newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Euphoria fades, problems remain for Bulgarian youth.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Euphoria fades, problems remain for Bulgarian youth.

text.p: A derelict basement by the construction site of the Sofia metro is an unpromising place for a nightclub, but the Muddy Cafe draws a regular crowd of young Bulgarians seeking escape from the gloom outside.
Taking its name from its surroundings, it offers the latest punk and techno hits to its disaffected clientele, whose future is as uncertain as that of the semi-abandoned building site.

Club DJ Ivailo Stanchev, known as Fozzy, was one of thousands of youngsters who joined month-long mass street protests which ousted the ex-communist government in February, paving the way for long-awaited change.
But as the euphoria died down, the 26-year-old found not much had changed for him and his friends.
"The faces are the same, their problems are the same, only the hits I play are new," he said.
Fozzy works at the Muddy from about midnight to 5 a.m. and also plays at private parties to make ends meet.

"Economic and political turmoil end at the Muddy's entrance, here we can forget about the uncertainty of life and just enjoy ourselves," said Krasi Petrov, who spends his nights at the club. "We are not running away from reality, this is our reality."
FUTURE IS A MESS FOR YOUTH
Petrov, who has finished technical school and works as a technician at a heating plant, says that on his miserable salary the club has one more important advantage -- cheap beer.
The Muddy Cafe was set up in the bare cellar of a derelict house in the early 1990s after the collapse of 45 years of totalitarian rule.

The ousting of communist dictator Todor Zhivkov at the end of 1989 freed young people from the relentless grip of the Communist Party and its youth organisation, the Komsomol, but brought new problems unknown to their predecessors.
Nearly 90,000 young Bulgarians left their country in 1990 alone, fleeing economic crisis and poor employment prospects. Almost all went to Western Europe or Canada.

Seven years later, after lip service to economic reform by eight mostly Socialist-dominated governments led the country to the biggest crisis in its recent history, the young people who stayed said their future seemed a total mess.
"Finding a job is difficult, but even if you get one the pay is miserable," said Petrov's friend Tomislava Sotirova, 22, who is finishing teacher training at Sofia University.
At the height of the economic crisis last winter, teachers were forced to stay at home because their daily transport fare added up to more than their salaries.
"I don't see any point in looking for a job... I want to leave this country, but where shall I go?" Sotirova said.
HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT BOOSTS DRUGS AND CRIME
One in eight Bulgarians is unemployed and the rate is set to rise further as the country introduces belated structural reforms.
Of the 56,207 jobless people who registered with the National Labour Exchange in May more than 23 percent were under 24 years old.

"The high long-term unemployment among young people provokes social insecurity and the destructive feeling of a lack of prospects, it fosters drug addiction and criminal activities," the United Nations Development Programme said in a report published last month.

The Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), which won an early general election in April, praised young people as the backbone of the winter protests but has been unable to offer concrete pledges for their future.

The UDF cabinet in office since mid-May has taken ambitious steps to stabilise the economy, improve welfare, fight crime and bring Bulgaria closer to the European Union and NATO. It also hopes to revive the Sofia metro, whose construction was begun in the 1980s.
"One of Bulgaria's main problems is the economic and physical survival of the young people," said Sasho Stoyanov, the UDF parliamentary deputy in charge of youth issues.
"This is the country's biggest asset -- a new generation which has not been deformed by communist ideology and can build a new Bulgaria within a united Europe," he said.
But the high hopes of the new government have yet to filter down to the dancers crammed in the bare basement of the Muddy Cafe. "They just want to listen to the music and forget," Fozzy said.
